items.summary: On Wednesday, security forces killed top Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) commander Lateef Bhat in an encounter inside a mosque in the Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir. The operation was framed by authorities as retaliation for an attack on Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) personnel that occurred seven days earlier. Bhat, described by security forces as the last active local terrorist in the Valley, had been located after an extensive search involving CCTV footage and repeated intelligence inputs; he refused to surrender despite appeals and was neutralised while trapped inside a mosque, with no damage caused to the structure. Union home minister Amit Shah praised the "coordinated efforts" of Jammu and Kashmir Police (JKP), Indian Army, CRPF, and intelligence agencies in neutralising Bhat. He also stated that one associate, Umar Nisar Dar, had been killed the day before. Director General of the CRPF GP Singh posted on X: "Congratulations, guys. Some dishes are best served cold, even in cold weather." The initial attack took place at a CRPF post in Akhran village on November 11, when two armed men opened fire and injured three personnel, one critically; ground verification later established that the attackers approached on foot from a nearby forested area rather than by motorcycle. CCTV footage examined between November 10 and 15 identified Bhat and Dar at multiple locations including Mir Bazar, Akhran, Hablish, and Kilam, documenting their reconnaissance before the attack and their flight afterward. Investigators found that Dar had allegedly provided shelter and logistical assistance to Bhat for five to six months; his family had filed a missing-person report after he disappeared, and officials said Dar joined The Resistance Front (TRF), an offshoot of LeT, after the November 11 attack. On November 16, following intelligence about two suspected terrorists near Laru bypass, security forces conducted another cordon-and-search operation; they evacuated students from two nearby schools before acting, and Dar was killed while Bhat escaped with alleged bullet injuries. On November 17, the search widened across dozens of villages using drones and sniffer dogs, though prolonged restrictions drew criticism from political leaders in Kashmir over hardship to ordinary residents. On November 18, contact with Bhat was re-established during an operation in Zangalpora village in the Devsar area; after he entered a mosque following appeals to surrender via video call involving him, the Kulgam SSP Anayat Ali Chowdhary, and the CEO of the 9 Rashtriya Rifles, police confirmed his death. The report is grounded entirely in statements from security officials and social media posts attributed to Amit Shah and GP Singh; no independent verification of these claims is provided.
items.title: Security forces neutralise LeT commander Lateef Bhat in Kulgam after CRPF post attack

items.summary:
According to ZDNET, Apple will impose daily usage limits on advanced tasks performed by Siri AI and Apple Intelligence beginning with the release of iOS 27.3, which is expected in early December. The limits apply only to server-side processing; basic commands such as setting timers or sending standard text messages remain free and unlimited because they are handled locally on the device. Advanced capabilities that will be subject to caps include multi-step requests using personal context like pulling email data to update a calendar, generating or editing images through Image Playground tools including Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing, Shortcuts relying on Apple Foundation Cloud and Cloud Pro Models, and third-party apps using Apple Foundation Models via Private Cloud Compute. The article notes that these server-side tasks can strain Apple's infrastructure when accessed simultaneously by many users at once.

The daily limits are tiered according to the user's iCloud+ subscription plan, with higher-paying plans receiving proportionally larger allowances relative to a baseline 'Standard Device Limit.' Users without a paid iCloud+ plan and those on the $0.99-per-month 50 GB plan will face only the standard limit. A $2.99-per-month 200 GB plan yields twice the standard usage, while a $9.99 per month 2 TB plan provides up to five times the standard limit. The $29.99 per month 6 TB plan grants up to 10 times the limit, and the top-tier $59.99 per month 12 TB plan offers up to 20 times the limit.

The article emphasizes that these limits are applied per device rather than per account, so a single iCloud+ subscription can be used across an iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Vision Pro without consuming additional quota. ZDNET frames this structure as potentially encouraging upgrades to pricier iCloud+ plans, while also explaining the practical rationale: advanced tasks depend on shared server-side AI models that must avoid overload when many users access them concurrently.

When a user reaches their daily allotment for a particular feature category, they will receive a notification. Basic tasks remain available at that point, but advanced functions are paused until the limit resets the following day. The article presents this as Apple's mechanism to manage server strain while nudging frequent users toward higher subscription tiers.
items.title: Apple Sets Daily Limits on Siri AI Use Starting with iOS 27.3

items.summary: Text strings discovered in Google's SIM Manager app suggest the company is preparing a feature called Fast Switch, which would let users share a single eSIM between two compatible Android phones. The code includes the phrase "Use a SIM on two phones," and according to Android Authority, both devices must be signed in under the same Google account for the feature to function. This mirrors Apple's iPhone Handoff, announced with iOS 27, which allows users to switch cellular service between two eSIM-enabled iPhones while keeping calls, messages, location services, and other Apple ID-synced information consistent across devices; some third-party apps such as banking, communications, or social media may also stay synced depending on each app's behavior. In the United States, iPhone Handoff is available for any US iPhone running iOS 27 with a T-Mobile or Verizon-provided eSIM, while AT&T does not currently support it. Fast Switch would appeal to people who regularly use two phones—such as business owners and digital creators separating work from personal devices—allowing them to avoid paying for two carrier service lines. However, users will still incur fees: T-Mobile charges $5/month for iPhone Handoff, while Verizon charges $10/month. Little information is currently available about Fast Switch's limitations, including which phones or carriers may not be compatible with the feature, as it remains in development and details are sparse beyond the code strings uncovered by Android Authority.
items.title: Google's Android Fast Switch: Sharing One eSIM Across Two Phones

items.summary:
The APEC CEO summit opened Wednesday in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where President Xi Jinping addressed delegates with a speech calling for freer trade and greater cooperation on artificial intelligence. He urged the elimination of trade and investment barriers while promoting inclusive development, technological innovation partnerships, digital economy cooperation, and green transitions. Russian President Vladimir Putin followed his address by criticizing Western powers as former hegemons, describing Europe's decline, and claiming that sanctions imposed after his 2022 invasion of Ukraine had backfired and strengthened Russia instead. The two leaders then held bilateral talks, according to Chinese and Russian state media.

The summit's most anticipated event is a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin scheduled for Thursday on the sidelines. China's foreign ministry said the three would discuss safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, while US officials indicate Trump is not expected to raise Russia's war in Ukraine directly. The talks could also cover Iran, denuclearisation, trade, AI, and nuclear weapons command systems. Observers have drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, though the Kremlin dismissed such parallels as mere political games.

Regarding North Korea, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump is willing to engage Kim Jong-un but did not confirm a meeting would occur in Shenzhen; APEC's Chinese hosts reported having no information on any bilateral talks. Analysts remain divided: some note that Putin may gain most from the trilateral by elevating Russia's standing, while others question what Kim might gain given his recent nuclear and missile progress.

On trade, Trump touted a 'very big trade deal' with the Philippines without details, though Manila announced no agreement; he is set to arrive in Shenzhen Wednesday evening. The US-Philippines alliance was described as stronger than ever, with expanded defense cooperation discussed. Trade tensions are expected to persist, particularly since the tenuous truce between Trump and Xi from their previous APEC summit expires in January.

Taiwan's participation remains sensitive given China's one-China principle; a Tuesday poll showed 71.8% of respondents supported Taiwan's involvement on equal terms. Meanwhile, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed he would join the leaders' family photo despite Putin's presence while making clear his opposition to Russia's invasion.

Trump has not yet arrived in Shenzhen and was last seen concluding talks with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., where he expressed no concern about the South China Sea situation. Delegates are working around the clock on a joint statement for Thursday, which all 21 APEC members reportedly agreed should ensure trade is both open and fair while addressing responsible AI use.

The summit's scope includes 21 member economies representing more than 50% of global GDP and home to about 2.7 billion people. Beyond the leaders' meetings, discussions are expected on AI governance amid concerns over military applications and rogue autonomous agents, building on an AI communication channel agreed between Trump and Xi in September.

The article notes several limitations: details remain unconfirmed for multiple events including Kim's attendance; Trump did not provide specifics on his trade deal claims; the Kremlin rejected Yalta comparisons as dismissive of their significance; and analysts hold conflicting views on what benefits various leaders might derive from these meetings. The piece also acknowledges that Beijing maintains neutrality on Ukraine while insisting Taiwan must adhere to its one-China principle, a position Taipei rejects.

Regarding AI specifically, Marina Zhang from the University of Technology Sydney noted the next step should be agreeing on reportable incidents and notification protocols without disclosing sensitive capabilities. Reports suggest Xi, Putin, and Trump may discuss using AI in nuclear weapons command systems, though Biden and Xi had previously agreed that human control over such decisions would remain paramount.

The article's framing draws heavily from state media sources for the leaders' statements and meeting confirmations, while incorporating analysis from various experts including Sydney Seiler of CSIS on Kim's potential attendance and Asia Society Policy Institute fellows on trade dynamics. The piece positions itself as a live blog with ongoing updates rather than a comprehensive retrospective.
items.title: APEC Summit in Shenzhen: Xi and Putin Open Talks; Trump-Xi-Putin Trilateral Meeting Set for Thursday

items.summary:
UK inflation rose slightly in October, with the headline consumer prices index reaching an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.5% in September and matching economists' forecasts. The rise was driven primarily by transport costs, particularly motor fuels; ONS figures showed transport prices climbing to 7.5% year on year, up from 6.6% the previous month. Petrol rose by an average of 5.2 pence per litre between September and October, while diesel increased by 7p a litre, with both rising more than in the same period last year. In contrast, food prices climbed at their slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September; chocolate prices fell by 2.9%, compared with a rise of 0.4% a year ago, as cocoa prices dropped sharply after the discounting of chocolate nearly doubled between September and October following lower-than-2024 levels amid a prior cocoa crisis. Factory gate prices rose at an annual rate of 5.1% in October, up from a revised figure of 4.7% in September.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food costs, increased by 2.8% in October, the same annual rate as in September. Services inflation was also unchanged at 3.7%. Felix Feather, an economist at Aberdeen fund manager, noted that while higher transportation fuel costs were the main driver of the increase, a recent decline in oil prices made it likely this would be partially reversed over November; he added that core and services inflation did not rise.

Separately, Nvidia announced Tuesday that its board chairman Harvey Jones stated the company does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. The remarks came during Nvidia's first quarterly earnings report since Huang's ouster amid allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees. On the same day, Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.84bn, doubling from the prior year period; this beat expectations despite the leadership turmoil.

Nvidia's stock fell more than 10% following Huang's departure, shedding hundreds of billions in value and reducing its valuation to $3.7tn. The company had reached an all-time-high valuation of nearly $6tn in October before a steady decline amid a broader AI slowdown. In other scheduled items, the agenda included European Central Bank financial stability report at 9am GMT, US Housing starts for October at 1.30pm GMT, ECB president Christine Lagarde speech at 2.25pm GMT, and US Federal Reserve minutes of its last meeting at 7pm GMT.
items.title: UK inflation rises to 3.6% on higher petrol prices; Nvidia confirms Jensen Huang's departure amid earnings

items.summary: UK inflation rose again in October, reaching 3.6% year-on-year according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), up from 3.5% in September. The increase was driven by higher petrol and diesel prices. Global oil prices have surged recently due to a US-Iran war, which has also been pushing up the cost of raw materials and goods leaving factories across the wider economy. In response to these price pressures, the Bank of England raised interest rates to 4%, marking its first rate increase in three years earlier that month. The bank signalled that further rises could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.
items.title: Higher fuel prices push UK inflation to 3.6%

items.summary: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October, up from 3.5% in September, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics measuring the consumer prices index. The increase was driven by rising energy prices triggered by the war in the Middle East and a 4% rise in the Ofgem energy price cap that took effect at the start of October. As households prepare for colder winter months, forecasters warn of a further inflation increase of as much as a quarter from January. Andy Burnham's government has pledged support for households facing renewed cost-of-living pressure while the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up worldwide inflation. At last month's budget, chancellor John Healey announced plans for a £100 winter handout to 20 million households to cushion the impact of the global economic situation. However, forecasters expect further inflation rises, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak close to 5% next year. Earlier this month Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%, warning that additional increases in borrowing costs may be needed to counter inflationary pressures stemming from the Iran war. Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year.
items.title: UK inflation rises to 3.6% amid energy price increases linked to Middle East conflict

items.summary: A cybersecurity firm called Calif has used artificial intelligence to uncover a critical flaw in Java, the world's third-largest programming language and one of its most widely deployed systems. The vulnerability, named Java4Shell, allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands within Java's memory system. According to the article, that adversary was OpenAI's recently released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public. Calif previously identified a critical flaw in PHP earlier this year; both discoveries were made with AI assistance. Professor Toby Walsh described the finding as an 'unlikely and serious' flaw because Java is designed specifically to manage and protect memory for users, making such vulnerabilities rare but dangerous when they occur. The article notes that overloading a system's memory remains one of the most common methods hackers use to exploit or crash systems. Oracle, which owns Java, has not acknowledged the bug directly but released a 'critical patch update' on Tuesday containing security vulnerability fixes; it is unclear whether any platforms or companies have been affected by this incident at this stage. The article places these events within a broader context of recent technology failures, including a massive Microsoft outage and a network failure that grounded all US flights, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stating there was 'zero evidence' the incidents are related. Separately, the National Security Agency reported its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to what it called 'scheduled routine maintenance,' though it did not specify whether this was linked to the Java bug; Apple also reported multiple service outages from an internal update. Dr Pedram Hayati warned that the flaw could compromise critical financial systems and organizations' data, noting that in Australia nearly every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data. The article highlights a growing reliance on AI in cybersecurity searches, pointing to OpenAI President Greg Brockman's announcement earlier in November of pivoting 25% of his company's staff toward cyber-security demands following the PHP discovery. Professor Alan Woodward noted the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites and had gone undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java over its roughly 12-year history since first release in 1995. Walsh emphasized that AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly than before, including ones so obscure they may have been undiscoverable by humans alone; the article also noted thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, recently reported trouble accessing services as these incidents exposed dependence on legacy online infrastructure across banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications. items.summary: Cambridge dictionary has selected "human" as its word of the year, defining it as "having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines." The choice reflects a growing emphasis on distinguishing human work from that of advanced AI systems. Colin McIntosh, an editor of the dictionary, said AI is "changing the way we talk about being human" and has led to the word being deployed to separate human output from computer-generated content. He noted that fears over what people may lose when outsourcing their thinking have prompted reconsideration of reliance on AI across fields ranging from top mathematicians to teachers of young children, pointing to a recent rise in compounds such as "human-made." Prof Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, added that AI revives age-old questions about identity: "who are we, what does it mean to be human?" She observed that while these answers have never been fixed or stable, asking them is a shared act. The selection follows broader debate over machine consciousness; evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins said he was "left with the overwhelming feeling that they are human," while sceptics argue there remains a vast difference between how a human brain evolves and how an AI system is built. Other words on Cambridge's shortlist included tech-related terms such as "agent" — describing an AI system that can operate without human control — and "analogues," relating to non-digital activities, alongside the non-tech contender "wholesome." The article also noted new dictionary additions including "looksmaxxing," associated with the online manosphere, and "aura farming," referring to performing actions intended to project an admirable personality. Separately, Collins named "mogging" — meaning to outperform or outshine someone or something — its word of the year earlier in 2026.
items.title: Cambridge Dictionary Names 'Human' Word of the Year for 2026

items.summary: On November 12, Poland's Ministry of Energy published recommendations urging grid operators to embed cybersecurity requirements into their operational rules and agreements with renewable energy producers and battery storage operators. The guidance is directed primarily at distribution system operators (DSOs) and the transmission system operator (TSO), aiming to strengthen security for solar and wind farms as well as battery energy storage systems connected to Poland's power system. Proposed measures include use of supported hardware and software, vulnerability management, secure network configurations, separation of operational technology (OT) systems from external networks, restricted remote access with virtual private networks and multifactor authentication where technically feasible, elimination of default passwords and unnecessary administrative interfaces, dedicated communication channels between installations and grid operators, network segmentation, redundant connections for critical installations, continuous monitoring where technically feasible, event logging, detection of unusual network activity, quarterly reviews of access privileges, reporting significant communication failures within 24 hours, and reporting cybersecurity incidents affecting communication, monitoring or control within four hours. The recommendations also call for harmonizing requirements across DSOs and the TSO, introducing compliance verification through periodic audits, ad hoc inspections and reporting obligations, transitional periods, corrective action plans, and alternative technical measures offering equivalent security levels; in cases of serious non-compliance by renewable energy producers, grid operators should consider refusing connections or terminating agreements after assessing legal grounds. Although not legally binding themselves, the recommendations could pave the way for cybersecurity requirements to become contractual conditions governing renewable energy grid connections. The initiative follows a coordinated cyberattack on Poland's solar infrastructure on December 29, 2025, which targeted around 30 renewable energy sites and compromised OT equipment including remote terminal units, protection relays and communications devices, disrupting communication between affected installations and DSOs while impairing remote monitoring and control though electricity generation continued. Related pv magazine coverage examined the cyber-insurance gap for battery storage and evolving solar cybersecurity threats; a separate event on December 3, 2026 (pv magazine Week Europe) is scheduled to explore real-world attack scenarios and protective strategies for solar assets. The recommendations are not legally binding in themselves but could inform future contractual conditions governing renewable energy grid connections. items.summary: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrived in Shenzhen on Tuesday afternoon ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders summit, where he says dialogue between nations is a 'good thing' even as Australia reaffirms its opposition to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Albanese indicated he would likely appear in the traditional APEC family photo alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, describing it as a matter of 'respect' for China as host and noting that if invited to an event he respects that while still making his position clear on Ukraine. He declined to follow former Prime Minister Tony Abbott's confrontational approach, saying he would not take lessons in diplomacy from the former prime minister who said he would 'shirt front' Putin at a 2014 G20 summit. Albanese characterised Moscow as 'a big power intervening in an illegal way,' framing Russia's actions against Ukraine as an attempt to assert its will while underestimating the Ukrainian people's conviction to fight for their national sovereignty, and insisted Australia's position remains unchanged. The annual gathering of 21 economies is expected to be overshadowed by a trilateral summit on Thursday between Putin, US President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping; Albanese said it was 'not up to Australia to determine who people have met with,' but reiterated that any solution or peace in Ukraine must be on 'Ukraine's terms.' Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned against the three leaders deciding his country's future without Kyiv at the table, likening the meeting to a modern-day Yalta conference. Albanese said he is due to sit down with Xi Jinping on Friday morning but would not foreshadow the issues he planned to raise. On domestic commitments, Albanese confirmed Labor's election promise to return the Port of Darwin lease into Australian hands before the 2028 election remains unchanged though he could not guarantee a timeline, noting there might be 'legal consequences and actions.' The port is leased to Chinese-owned company Landbridge in what has become a sensitive issue in the bilateral relationship. He also signalled continued pressure on China to remove barriers to Australian agricultural exports after tariffs exceeded an annual quota on beef, stating Australia would 'rather not have any quotas on Australian goods anywhere in the world,' while noting strong demand for Australian beef demonstrates appeal to Chinese consumers following a visit to a Shenzhen supermarket stocking local products including apples, cherries, beef and lobster. Albanese said trade with China is important for Australian jobs and economic growth.
items.title: Albanese arrives in Shenzhen ahead of APEC summit and Putin talks

items.summary: The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week. Separately, US President Donald Trump will also meet Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China. Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues; maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives. Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce. Over the next two years, Kim expects "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today." Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad: domestically he faces becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections, while internationally damage to relations with allies, weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage. Zhang believes these factors have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities. Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship. She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side; while the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win for both governments. Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals, but Tee believes China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs. She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls. With another meeting between the two leaders expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting. Regarding Russia's agenda, Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate, which could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine. "Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three." Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue. She summarized each leader's aim as: "Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," expecting each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions. On Ukraine mediation, Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end; Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing. An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective: "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so. Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests," arguing that the Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and weakened, and that the United States has also lost moral authority as alliances built around Washington have eroded. He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries; at the same time China does not want Ukraine to be defeated because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing. For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly, instead waiting for a more favorable moment and then potentially stepping in as a neutral mediator to maximize its gains. On Iran, W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran. The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives." Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position; "China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," and Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region. No visual was selected because the document offers only qualitative expert assessments rather than comparable numeric relationships suitable for charting; figures such as $30 billion (€27.3 billion) are embedded within narrative claims about tariff cuts and cannot stand alone as a plotted comparison, so prose is the appropriate form.
items.title: Expert expectations for Trump–Xi and US–China–Russia trilateral talks at APEC Shenzhen summit

items.summary: According to an India Today report, 37-year-old Akshita Jain has left a lucrative corporate career—backed by an MBA from IIM Bengaluru and roles with Fiat, Mercedes-Benz, and Volkswagen—to embrace Jain asceticism. In her most recent position at Volkswagen, she reportedly earned an annual compensation package of ₹50 lakh. The turning point in her transition came during AI initiatives at work; Akshita grew concerned about the environmental footprint of large data centres, specifically land excavation and harm to microscopic soil organisms. She said this realization aligned with Jain ahimsa (non-violence toward all living beings), prompting renunciation. Her 61-year-old mother, Shiromani Bajaj—retired chief manager at IOCL after a 37-year career ending in October 2025—is joining her. Following her husband's death and household duties, Shiromani reportedly turned to Jain spirituality through close association with sadhvis and completed religious observances and austerities. The Gurugram-based duo is receiving guidance from Sadhvi Purnapragyashree. A traditional varghoda procession was scheduled in Jodhpur, setting up their formal diksha ceremony in Chennai on February 25—a transition formally renouncing worldly attachments to become ascetics. The item includes boilerplate about Livemint's coverage areas and editorial team; the only figures with numeric values are Akshita's ₹50 lakh salary, Shiromani's 37-year tenure ending October 2025, and the February 25 ceremony date.
items.title: Corporate professionals renounce careers to become Jain ascetics amid AI-driven environmental concerns

items.summary: The Jammu and Kashmir Police reported that Lateef Bhat, a commander of the Lashkar-e-Taiba terror group, was killed in a gunfight in Kulgam on Wednesday. According to reports from The Hindu, senior superintendent of police Anayat Ali Choudhary said security forces had 'a long conversation' with the militant by phone before engaging him. Choudhary stated that they asked Bhat to surrender but he refused, and added that they exercised maximum restraint because he was hiding inside a mosque. Central Reserve Police Force Director General GP Singh commented on social media that 'some dishes are best served cold, even in cold weather.' Bhat carried a bounty of Rs 15 lakh and had been wanted for his alleged involvement in an attack on the Central Reserve Police Force on November 11, during which three security personnel were killed. He was also allegedly involved in attacks in Anantnag and Kulgam districts in July, according to reports. The article is written by Nachiket Deuskar and edited by Sara Varghese. No casualty figures for the engagement itself are reported beyond the three CPF personnel killed in the November 11 attack Bhat was wanted over. No details on how many security forces were involved or injured during Wednesday's gunfight are provided, nor is there confirmation of whether any militants besides Bhat died.
items.title: Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat killed in Kulgam gunfight

items.summary: A report titled 'Friendship in an Online-Offline World: Digital Life, Connection and Wellbeing,' produced by public polling firm Gallup and the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children's Hospital, finds that more than one-third (33 percent) of Gen Z rely on AI for companionship. The reliance was higher among daily AI users, spiking to 50 percent, and reached 42 percent among those with online-only friends. Rather than measuring screen time alone, the report examined who young people connect with and how these relationships affect their social lives and mental health. Researchers distinguished three modes of close connection: in-person friendships, friendships that started IRL but are sustained online, and online-only friendships where a person has never met their friend in real life. The survey was conducted between May and August, sampling 15,925 people aged 15 to 22 across 16 countries. It found that Gen Z benefits more from in-person relationships than digital ones, even though nearly half of young people in the US have at least one close online-only friend. In-person friendships were rated highest for 'strength and support' and associated with the most positive emotional experiences, while those relying on online-only friends or AI may face higher odds of loneliness. David Bickham, research director of the Digital Wellness Lab, said he does not view this as a major deficit but rather young people growing up in an age of AI; 'I don't necessarily see it as, oh, these kids have some sort of major deficit and are looking to AI.' He noted that while AI may fill a social gap, loneliness specifically is something online relationships cannot fully compensate for. When maintaining affiliations with online-only friends, Instagram and Discord were the top platforms in the US, surprisingly not TikTok. Bickham observed that boys who report higher social anxiety are less likely to make connections but still seek out chatbots when lonely; young women most commonly mentioned social media as their way of cultivating connection. Recent debates over teen screen time have centered on whether digital devices drive a youth mental health crisis or if concerns are overstated, with critics arguing blunt measures overlook content type. Social media bans and age-restriction policies for minors took effect in Australia and the UK this year; in the US, where state legislators introduced bills to curb addictive design features, a majority of Americans support banning kids under 16 from using social media, according to Pew Research. Jon-Patrick Allem, an associate professor at the Rutgers School of Public Health who wrote last year in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine, argued that research has focused on 'blunt measures of screen time' and would 'treat all content consumed online as uniform,' calling this approach deficient and urging a new agenda investigating actual content. Bickham agreed it was important to look beyond surface-level analysis at the nature of relationships formed while online; 'A more important finding is the quality of relationship.' A previous Digital Wellness Lab report mapped AI use among teenagers in the US, Brazil, and France, finding teens aged 13 to 17 turned to AI for personal advice and creative work as well as companionship. While researchers are wary of classifying this as a permanent shift, they say it signals growing reliance on AI companionship within broader digital social engagement; 'It wouldn't be surprising if AI companionship becomes more common over the next five years,' says Andrew Dugan, a principal researcher at Gallup. However, whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely or whether AI reinforces those feelings remains an important question for future research.
items.title: Over a Third of Gen Z Rely on AI for Companionship

items.summary:
A Border Security Force (BSF) personnel was detained on Tuesday by Bangladesh's border guarding force after he reportedly "inadvertently" crossed the unfenced international border around noon, according to The Indian Express. He returned safely in the evening following a meeting between commanders from both sides.

The security personnel is reported to have crossed the border from Meghalaya's Jowai into Bangladesh's Sylhet district, venturing approximately 200 yards across it, per India Today NE. At the time of his detention, he was reportedly carrying a walkie-talkie, an Indian Small Arms System rifle, and a pump-action gun, according to The Shillong Times.

Videos shared on social media showed two Border Guard Bangladesh personnel along with several residents accompanying the Indian constable after he crossed into Bangladesh. In one video, he is seen being taken away by Bangladeshi personnel on a civilian motorcycle, per The Indian Express. After the Border Security Force took cognisance of these videos, senior officers deployed in Meghalaya contacted their Bangladeshi counterparts and called for a flag meeting, according to The Shillong Times.

The Border Security Force guards a 4,096-km-long stretch of border between India and Bangladesh. All details are drawn from the reporting cited within this item.
items.title: Indian BSF personnel detained after crossing into Bangladesh

items.summary: Chief Minister DK Shivakumar inaugurated the 29th Bengaluru Tech Summit, themed 'AI and Beyond', on Tuesday, outlining Karnataka's ambition to expand into artificial intelligence, deep technology, semiconductor manufacturing, and biotechnology. The state earned approximately USD 173 billion in software exports last year, accounting for two out of every five dollars India received through software and services exports; it also drew USD 9.4 billion in FDI equity inflows in the first half of FY 2025-26, representing 26.7 per cent of India's total inflows during that period. More than 1,000 Global Capability Centres have chosen Bengaluru as their base, while over 30 new GCCs brought investments exceeding USD 1 billion into the state in 2025 alone. Karnataka hosts more than 24,000 recognised startups and nearly two out of every five unicorns nationally; Bengaluru ranks among the world's leading startup ecosystems and is second in Asia for AI-native startups. Startups in Bengaluru raised USD 4.4 billion—nearly matching the combined funding of the next five Indian cities—with Karnataka-based ventures raising a cumulative USD 79 billion, and women-led Bengaluru ventures attracting USD 13.4 billion. On talent, Shivakumar said Bengaluru holds nearly half of India's AI and machine learning workforce, with plans for an AI University and an AI Hub; an additional Centre of Excellence at IIIT Raichur would extend AI applications to the 13 districts of North Karnataka across agriculture, healthcare, education, and small businesses. The proposed Bengaluru Robotics and AI Innovation Zone (BRAINZ) is set to further strengthen the ecosystem. Under Nipuna Karnataka, Rs 300 crore has been earmarked for reskilling, with 33,000 people—including women returning after career breaks—made industry-ready. In semiconductors, the state hosts more than 100 fabless companies and three out of every five engineers in India's semiconductor capability centres are based in Bengaluru; Karnataka accounts for one-fifth of India's electronics exports, with companies committing over Rs 23,000 crore to research, development, and manufacturing in Bengaluru and Mysuru. Four electronics manufacturing clusters are being developed between Dharwad and Mysuru under the state's electronics system design and manufacturing policy. The bioeconomy was valued at USD 39.2 billion last year—about one-fifth of India's total and more than 10 per cent of the state's economy—with initiatives underway in marine biotechnology, agriculture, healthcare, genome editing, and gene therapy. On the summit itself, participation rose to more than 75 countries from 57 last year; exhibitors nearly doubled, and business visitor participation is expected to rise by about a third. Startup support continues through ELEVATE, which has provided equity-free grants to 1,500 startups over the past decade; under ELEVATE NxT, 33 deep-tech startups received Rs 30 crore since last year; the proposed Innoverse programme aims to support 35 growth-stage ventures over five years; and Rs 25 crore has been earmarked to procure solutions developed by startups.
items.title: Karnataka Targets Global AI and Semiconductor Hub Amid Software Export Strength

items.summary: A political controversy has emerged after public remarks revealed private moments of parental affection that occurred during meals at a book launch. The ruling party criticised these disclosures, arguing they conflict with Indian cultural values and household respect. Opposition figures defended the affection, linking it instead to traditional religious values. As election season approaches, the debate escalated online across social platforms, expanding into broader discussions about family respect, cultural norms, and political expression. A related controversy surrounds permission to light the Karthigai Deepam lamp at the Deepa Thoon pillar amid ongoing legal and religious disputes. Separately, the Vishwanath Dham corridor's opening in Varanasi has reportedly boosted local commerce and jobs across multiple sectors including tourism, crafts, and transport. The BJP is preparing for Uttar Pradesh assembly elections with a Jan Ashirwad Yatra and district meetings to gather grassroots feedback, while rival parties are also intensifying their campaigns.
items.title: Political leaders clash over private displays of parental affection during public event

items.summary: A political controversy has emerged concerning permission to light the Karthigai Deepam lamp at the Deepa Thoon pillar. The state government has approached the Supreme Court seeking relief, while opposition leaders argue that the ritual should be permitted at the designated site. Tensions have been heightened by the pillar's proximity to a dargah. Although a single-judge bench of the High Court had authorized the lighting of the lamp, local police refused permission on procedural grounds. With the Karthigai festival approaching, concerns about unrest persist amid ongoing political and religious disputes over worship rights.
items.title: Political dispute over Karthigai Deepam lamp lighting at Deepa Thoon pillar

items.summary: India has developed its first indigenous vaccine against the H5N1 avian influenza virus, commonly known as bird flu, to strengthen preparedness for poultry outbreaks. The inactivated vaccine was created by ICAR-NIHSAD (National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases) and targets the H5N1 virus of clade 2.3.2.1a, which has been responsible for most bird flu outbreaks in chickens. Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan is set to dedicate the vaccine at NIHSAD's facility in Bhopal on November 20. According to ICAR-NIHSAD, a single dose provides protection for up to six months and makes the vaccine suitable for layer and breeder chickens; until now, no specific commercial vaccine had been available against this clade of H5N1 virus. The development comes amid fresh bird flu outbreaks in parts of India, including Tamil Nadu's Cuddalore district, where H5N1 infection was confirmed in November following sudden bird deaths at poultry farms and 35,647 birds died as of November 13; authorities initiated culling within a one-kilometre radius, with around 40,000 chickens subsequently reported culled. Andhra Pradesh also reported an outbreak in October in Anantapur district's Siddarampuram village in Bukkarayasamudram mandal, prompting the state government to declare infected and surveillance zones and restrict poultry movement. Bird flu, or highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), can cause severe disease and high mortality among poultry; since it was first detected in India in 2006, more than 500 combined outbreaks of H5N1 and H5N8 subtypes have been reported. The government says the H5N1 clade 2.3.2.1a strain has also been detected in different animal species, including mammals, as well as in three human cases; separately, the World Health Organization has reported 1,003 human cases of H5N1, including 479 deaths, across 25 countries since 2003. The indigenous vaccine is expected to add another tool to India's efforts to control outbreaks, alongside surveillance, testing, biosecurity and culling.
items.title: India develops its own H5N1 vaccine amid fresh bird flu outbreaks

items.summary: State Food Safety officials seized 1,240 kg of edible oil from Bolas Agro Private Limited on November 17 at the Baikampady Industrial Area in Dakshina Kannada district. The seizure followed alleged misbranding and labelling violations: raw groundnut oil was procured from Challakere in Chitradurga district, then repackaged and sold as cold pressed groundnut oil. The seized stock comprised 11 boxes of groundnut oil (10 kg per box), 30 cans of groundnut oil (35 litres per can), and 4 boxes of coconut oil (20 kg per box). Officials stated the operation was conducted by the Food Safety and Drug Administration Department.
items.title: Karnataka Seizes 1,240 kg of Edible Oil Over Misbranding in Dakshina Kannada

items.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said authorities had found no evidence linking recent disruptions at Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and major banks to cyberattacks or foreign governments, stating that 'We are not under systemic attack' and dismissing an alleged Iranian plan for an imminent threat on Washington, DC. Russian President Vladimir Putin met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen ahead of a three-way talk with US President Donald Trump; Putin argued economic coercion is 'a thing of the past,' saying sanctions could slow but not stop growth, and expected Thursday's talks to be useful. The Quad held its first leader-level meeting in more than two years in Manila, bringing together Trump, Australian PM Anthony Albanese, Indian PM Narendra Modi and Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi; Trump called them 'the four corners of a free, open, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific.' In the Iran war, Iran's army said it launched drones at US installations at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem Air Base, with Kuwait engaging but not confirming a hit; Bahrain intercepted several Iranian attacks early Wednesday after Iran's Revolutionary Guard targeted a radar system there on Monday. On Tuesday, American aircraft struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island as US-Iran talks remain stalled over safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Britain imposed sanctions under Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband targeting eight construction and property firms involved in illegal settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank and a group blocking aid to Gaza; this was the first package since September's reset of the UK's approach, intended to disrupt their finance flows. Separately, US immigration authorities detained former world boxing champion Jorge Linares at El Paso International Airport after he overstayed his authorized stay; ICE spokeswoman Leticia Zamarripa said he entered on Oct. 26, 2023 with temporary permission and is held at the El Paso Processing Center, though lawyers say he is in the country legally. French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo announced he will challenge Gianni Infantino in FIFA's presidential election on March 18, 2027, citing decisions that damaged football's image; UEFA said European associations had unanimously backed his bid, while Infantino has led FIFA since 2016. A Spanish court sentenced a Real Oviedo supporter to 11 months for racially abusing Kylian Mbappe during an August 2025 La Liga match, fining him and suspending the sentence on condition he stay away from stadiums hosting official events for two years; Real Madrid took part as private prosecutor. Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI is set to launch at midnight, 13 years after the last main installment; Sensor Tower estimated players had placed 14.9 million digital preorders by Nov. 16, spending about $1.45 billion, while Newzoo projected global sales could reach $3.25 billion to $5.2 billion by end of launch week, its biggest opening on record. Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue doubled from a year earlier to $115.84 billion in its first earnings since co-founder Jensen Huang's departure; board chair Harvey Jones said the company did not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO, and Huang apologized for his mistakes while saying he would return if the board decided it was best. Google found no evidence of a widespread Gmail disruption despite thousands of reports by 12 noon ET (Downdetector recorded more than 2,800 problems), with most complaints about receiving emails; its Workspace Status Dashboard listed no active disruptions as of 1.45 pm ET. Gold fell nearly 1.5% to $3,792 an ounce and silver dropped 2.6% to $46.12 amid a stronger dollar and prospects of further Fed rate hikes; St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said several more increases would likely be needed before spring, while New York Fed President John Williams noted inflation remained above the central bank's 2% target. Gold has lost more than a quarter of its value since the US-Iran war began in late February, as investors await Wednesday's Fed meeting minutes.
items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 18, 2026

items.summary: Residents of New Smyrna Beach, Florida, reported a sigh of relief after the Volusia Sheriff's Office apprehended 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell for allegedly leading deputies on an electric bicycle chase. On November 13, while riding along the beach in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h limit), Mitchell was clocked traveling at 16 mph (26 km/h). A deputy attempted to stop him; he reportedly responded with a middle finger and choice words before continuing on his way. He then rode onto city streets, allegedly riding against traffic, before returning home where he resisted arrest by grabbing a golf cart and refusing to release it. Mitchell was taken into custody facing four charges: felony fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, resisting an officer without violence, speeding on the beach, and riding outside the designated beach driving area; his bond was set at $4,000. In commentary attributed to Electrek, the author acknowledged that e-bike riders should not ignore traffic laws or endanger pedestrians, noting Mitchell reportedly rode recklessly around beachgoers including children. The author argued the incident is absurd: a 75-year-old man riding an electric bicycle at 16 mph became subject to a police pursuit and felony charges, while multi-ton vehicles routinely kill and injure people as an accepted cost of modern transportation. Citing that 40,000 people die every year in the US from car violence, the author contrasted this with e-bikes contributing far less harm or death yet being treated as a great transportation menace. The author also endorsed legitimate concerns about dangerous riding, especially teenagers on high-powered electric dirt bikes and e-motos at 40 mph (64 km/h) down sidewalks and bike paths, which are not electric bicycles but have been misclassified, creating real problems for everyone. Concluding that Mitchell's alleged behavior after being stopped did not help his case, the author maintained the larger point remains: road-safety priorities have become wildly distorted, normalizing car dangers while treating comparatively low-speed e-bikes as an existential threat to public safety; sensible enforcement of e-bike rules is supported, but perspective should be applied rather than turning a 1 mph beach ride into the crime of the century. The author closed by noting that if such a slow electric bicycle ride were among our most pressing transportation-safety concerns, there would be good news about road conditions, though unfortunately none exists today.
items.title: Florida man leads police on slow e-bike chase; Electrek weighs in on road-safety priorities

items.summary: A special police team rescued a 12-year-old girl who had been left asleep in the backseat of her family's vehicle after it was stolen near Guduvanchery in Tamil Nadu, and arrested the suspected thief on Wednesday. The incident occurred when the victim's parents parked their car outside a local cloud kitchen to grab a quick meal, leaving the engine and air conditioning running to keep the child comfortable while she slept. A 46-year-old man named Raj Mohan took advantage of the unattended vehicle by slipping into the driver's seat and driving off with the sleeping girl in the backseat. Acting on the complaint, police launched an intensive search and flashed alerts across neighbouring police limits in Kancheepuram and Chengalpattu districts. Officers near the Kuvananchery checkpost spotted a suspicious car approaching, signalled it to stop, and upon halting discovered the 12-year-old girl inside, crying and visibly traumatised. Police rescued the child and handed her safely over to her parents, while taking Raj Mohan into custody on the spot. During a search of the vehicle, officers recovered gold jewellery that had been looted from it. Investigators were reportedly conducting a thorough inquiry to determine whether the accused had other motives or was involved in similar offenses. The article notes an 'Also Read' link referencing unrelated crime statistics reports for Bengaluru and another Tamil Nadu case involving a murder convict, neither of which pertains to this incident. The source is marked as untrusted text; all reported details are drawn directly from that reporting without independent verification beyond what the item states itself. No specific time of day or exact date (beyond 'Wednesday') was provided for when the theft occurred or the rescue took place. No further details were given about how much gold jewellery was recovered, nor any confirmed findings on whether Raj Mohan had prior involvement in similar crimes—these remain open questions pending investigation. The article does not state where exactly Guduvanchery is located relative to Kancheepuram and Chengalpattu districts beyond that alerts spanned those neighbouring police limits. No information about the parents' identities, occupations, or how they reported the theft was included in the item. The child's name was never disclosed by the reporting. Raj Mohan's occupation before becoming an 'on-call driver,' his prior criminal record (if any), and the circumstances under which he obtained driving access to the vehicle were not addressed beyond the allegation that he stole the idling car. No official charges, court proceedings, or bail status for the accused are mentioned in this item. The article does not specify whether the recovered gold jewellery belonged to the family or was otherwise stored in the vehicle at the time of theft. No statements from police officials, parents, or the child were quoted directly; all claims derive solely from unnamed 'police' and 'they said' attributions within the untrusted source text. The item does not indicate whether the car itself sustained damage during the theft or was later recovered intact beyond its use in the crime. No information about how long the vehicle remained stolen before being stopped by police is provided, only that officers spotted it approaching the checkpost after alerts were issued. This reporting presents a single account of one incident without offering alternative explanations for why the car was left running unattended or any commentary on broader patterns of such thefts in the region beyond the two tangential 'Also Read' links to unrelated reports.
items.title: Police rescue 12-year-old girl from stolen car in Guduvanchery; driver arrested

items.summary: In an interview with Anadolu Agency on the sidelines of COP31's second week in Antalya, Türkiye, on 18 November 2026, Zaghloul Samhan, head of the Palestinian Environment Quality Authority, called for the summit to explicitly recognize countries under occupation and crisis as highly vulnerable. He argued that developed nations should pay for their climate effects while developing countries benefit from the resulting finance, urging delegates to prioritize adaptation over emissions cuts given developing states' minimal share of global emissions and disproportionate exposure to climate impacts. Samhan stressed Palestine's core priority is giving such countries precedence in assessing resource needs and financing, easing access to financial resources as well as environmental and climate funds. He specifically requested that Palestine gain access to the Global Environment Facility (GEF) project funds one day, while procedures for accessing the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and other environmental funds be streamlined; both mechanisms serve as main financial arms of the UN climate framework but political restrictions have barred Palestine from major GEF project funds, and GCF financing has remained limited due to lengthy accreditation and project-approval hurdles. Unlocking these funds would allow Palestine to carry out adaptation and mitigation projects outlined in its nationally determined contributions (NDCs). Samhan also underscored the urgent need for resources to rebuild Gaza's devastated environmental infrastructure, noting that around 97% of the enclave's agricultural land is either contaminated or inaccessible to Palestinians; a joint UN Food and Agriculture Organization and UNOSAT satellite assessment confirmed only 3% of Gaza's cropland remained accessible and undamaged as of August 2026, while a World Bank–UN–EU report estimates agriculture and food-system reconstruction needs at nearly $10.5 billion. He said the scale of destruction requires sweeping reconstruction across virtually every environmental sector—destroyed wastewater networks and treatment plants, renewable energy facilities, solid waste systems, medical and hazardous waste facilities, plus water infrastructure such as groundwater wells, desalination plants, distribution networks and reservoirs—and flagged Wadi Gaza's nature reserve as one of the most polluted areas in Gaza. Damaged sewage and waste systems have left raw wastewater and debris flowing into the Mediterranean, contaminating coastal and marine ecosystems; Samhan warned enormous financial backing will be needed to restore basic services, farmland and natural environment. Despite obstacles, he expressed optimism about progress at the summit, citing Türkiye's COP31 presidency as a source of support and praising its hosting as one of the best COPs he ever attended.
items.title: Palestinian environment chief calls for COP31 climate finance access and Gaza reconstruction funding

items.summary: On Thursday, Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump are meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. The article frames this gathering as a rare chance for the leaders of the world's three major powers to exchange views directly on global issues, drawing comparisons to the 1945 Yalta conference when Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin divided the world into spheres of influence after World War II. However, it argues that Shenzhen is not 'Yalta 2.0' nor an isolated episode: in May this year Xi hosted back-to-back visits by Trump and Putin to Beijing; Trump reciprocated by hosting Xi in Washington in September and meeting with Putin in Alaska last year. Taken together, these developments signal a broader shift away from the post-Cold War emphasis on global institutions and multilateral consultations toward a more personalised form of great-power management that is likely 'the new normal': a world in which China, Russia, and the US act as an informal steering committee for global affairs, with Europe and other middle powers increasingly on the sidelines. The article notes these three remain strategic competitors but share an understanding of conducting international politics through direct engagement among few major powers rather than institutions or coalitions; this is described not as a formal alliance—even between China and Russia—or a coordinated redesign of the international system, but as a common instinct toward great-power management in which major powers enjoy special rights and privileged voices while limiting others' involvement. As evidence, it cites that Russia and the US just concluded a third round of peace talks this year in Abu Dhabi towards ending the Ukraine war, during which Ukraine was part of discussions but European negotiators were not; Trump has flagged as possible a new security framework for Europe modelled after Cold War spheres of influence, saying the US is working on a big deal to end the war that would include 'all of Europe'; and Jared Kushner said Washington wanted Europe in the process while adding finding someone who could credibly speak for Europe might be harder than persuading Russia to include them. Xi's agreement to join the Shenzhen trilateral summit risks legitimising Europe's exclusion, even though Ukraine is not on the agenda; this looks awkward for China given Xi's repeated emphasis on multipolarity and criticism of Cold War-style politics dominated by a few major powers, and Beijing's previous stress that Europe should be 'at the table' for Ukraine discussions. The article observes that despite these tensions, China's Foreign Ministry described the summit as having 'groundbreaking significance,' with the three leaders to 'exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations,' suggesting Beijing accepts a diplomacy model centred on major powers to the exclusion of others—an uncomfortable reality for Europe, which remains one of the world's largest economic and technological centres but struggles to translate that weight into a unified strategic voice. Turning to middle powers, the article argues their return to relevance does not mean they are irrelevant: European nations, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, and key Southeast Asian nations may lack the military capabilities or geopolitical heft to alter the distribution of power in the international system, but they retain institutions, networks, and coalitions that can help shape rules, sustain institutions, and build partnerships capable of constraining larger states. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's call for closer middle-power cooperation reflects this logic—rather than choosing sides in great-power rivalry, he has recognised the necessity to 'stop pretending, to name the reality' while 'building coalitions that work – issue by issue, with partners who share enough common ground to act together.' The article concludes that as global power concentrates in fewer leaders' hands, middle powers have stronger incentives to cooperate; they are unlikely to decide the overall direction of world order but can still influence the rules, norms, and institutions through which it operates. The central question raised by Shenzhen is therefore not whether a handful of major powers will continue exercising disproportionate influence—they will—but how the rest of the world will respond.
items.title: Xi-Trump-Putin Shenzhen Summit and the Rise of Great-Power Management

items.summary: According to a Bloomberg report cited in the article, Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress announced at the company's latest earnings call that it is no longer shipping licensed Hopper datacenter chips to China and does not expect such sales to contribute to future results. During the third quarter, Nvidia sold approximately $2.4 billion worth of these licensed Hopper products in China; however, its forward guidance excludes any further licensed Hopper datacenter shipments. This decision marks a sharp departure from founder Jensen Huang's long-standing advocacy for expanded access to the Chinese market and his repeated lobbying for US government approval to sell advanced AI processors there. Previously, Nvidia had pushed Washington for permission to export Blackwell chips to China; while that request was not approved, the Trump administration later permitted sales of Hopper-based H200 processors, which are older than Nvidia's latest Rubin-generation products. Kress did not explain why the company is ending shipments to China, though her comments suggest Nvidia is stepping away from a business that generated billions in recent revenue. The move coincides with tightening US export restrictions: the Trump administration has introduced measures aimed at increasing scrutiny of processor exports and limiting sales to overseas data centers that could give Chinese companies remote access to advanced AI infrastructure. Reflecting these concerns, Harvey Jones—appointed Nvidia's first board chair last week—noted that changing national security dynamics are significantly impacting the market and warned that the company's next CEO must navigate them carefully. In response, Nvidia announced a dedicated board-level committee focused on national security and export-control issues, signaling greater geopolitical influence over future business decisions. Separately, Microsoft remained committed to its partnership with Nvidia; CEO Satya Nadella expressed confidence in the management team under interim CEO Colette Kress—who previously worked at Microsoft—and emphasized that Microsoft is continuing to scale deployment of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin processors, describing it as a critical project for both companies amid their close relationship during the AI boom. items.summary: Nvidia announced that it is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center chips to China, even though the company had won approval from the US government last year to sell a version of that model there. Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim chief executive officer, told analysts during an earnings call on Tuesday that the firm sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper data center products to China in the third quarter. However, she said its future guidance includes no such licensed Hopper shipments and confirmed it is ending them. Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments were being cut off. The move represents a notable shift for a company that has spent years seeking expanded business with Chinese customers. Jensen Huang, who was ousted as CEO last week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, had been Nvidia's most vocal advocate for exporting chips to China. Huang departed after disclosing an affair with a woman now under investigation by the US government over potential ties to China's spy agency and possible help smuggling chips there; Beijing has denied attempting to spy on him. On Monday, the Trump administration moved to apply greater scrutiny to processor exports to several countries and to limit chip sales abroad when data center buyers plan to give Chinese companies remote access to advanced AI chips and servers. Nvidia had earlier pushed for permission to sell more advanced Blackwell chips to China; that request was never granted, but President Donald Trump approved the sale of Hopper processors known as H200s, which are two generations behind Nvidia's leading Rubin family of chips, reflecting the strong relationship Huang built with Trump. Harvey Jones, appointed Nvidia's first chair last week, said the board recognizes it is 'living in a world' where national security dynamics are reshaping its marketplace and that its next CEO must navigate those waters carefully. The company also announced forming a board committee focused on national security and export controls, boosted its sales forecast for next year, promised to improve access to critical supplies, and downplayed speculation about Huang's return. (Source: Bloomberg) Note the article does not state why Nvidia ended shipments beyond citing shifting national security dynamics; it attributes that framing to company leadership rather than providing independent detail on the decision itself.
items.title: Nvidia Halts Licensed Hopper Chip Shipments to China Despite Prior US Approval

items.summary: Former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang said on Nov 17 that he wanted his job back, despite resigning over an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. In his first statement since stepping down last week, Huang wrote: "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO." He added that if the Board decides his return serves shareholders, employees, the company, and America, he would be honored to come back. The scandal has battered shares of Nvidia, which lost US$700 billion (S$902 billion) in market value since it broke; Huang is set to face questions from US lawmakers on Dec 1 over national security concerns. His fall triggered calls for his return from Elon Musk and other entrepreneurs, and President Donald Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Huang back at Nvidia while downplaying the spy allegations. On Nov 16, Washington announced new restrictions on AI chip exports that drew condemnation from Beijing, just as talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping were set to begin this week at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Under the new rules, data centres worldwide will need a US licence to supply large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau, or other countries under US arms embargoes; licences are also required to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil over diversion risk. The changes target a loophole that let Chinese firms rent AI computing power from data centres abroad running on US hardware not available for export to China. Huang's lover Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud firm under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia chips in circumvention of export controls; she is unrelated to the 63-year-old chief. Nvidia's Nov 17 third-quarter results, scheduled for 5pm ET (6am on Nov 18 in Singapore), will be the first presented by interim CEO Colette Kress. Jacob Bourne of Emarketer said a business-as-usual tone from her would likely not be well received; analysts expect scrutiny over whether she will slow Huang's aggressive investment strategy, Nvidia's future sales guidance, and its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore. The situation carries wider stakes: Nvidia backs major labs including Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Nov 19. AFP reported that Huang sounded contrition in his statement, saying "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life."
items.title: Jensen Huang seeks return as Nvidia prepares first earnings since scandal and new US chip curbs
