items.summary: Labour's North Northumberland MP David Smith has urged Northumberland County Council to accelerate the processing of heating oil support payments as global conflicts drive energy prices higher. Approximately 23,000 homes in Northumberland rely on oil systems because they are not connected to the mains gas supply. Unlike gas, which is protected by the Ofgem Energy Price Cap, oil tank-filling costs have risen sharply for households. A freedom of information request from 21 September showed that just over a third of applicants had received funding: Smith reported 328 applications with only 112 approved and total payments amounting to £36,123. The Conservative-led council responded by citing more recent figures showing significantly higher approval rates almost two months later, stating that more than 160 applicants and 40 venues had been supported and that there was no backlog for residents seeking assistance. A spokesperson explained that those not receiving support are applicants who have failed to demonstrate their household is vulnerable or struggling due to low income. The government provided £5m to the county council through its Crisis and Resilience fund in April, including almost £500,000 earmarked for households facing heating oil costs. Bamburgh Conservative councillor Guy Renner-Thompson, who has a home using a heating oil system, called on the government for additional financial support, noting that the council fully expected to spend the entire £498,459 heating oil allocation.
items.title: Northumberland MP urges council to speed up heating oil support payments amid soaring energy prices

items.summary: Anton Osika, CEO of Lovable, a generative-AI startup recently valued at over $13 billion and flush with investment cash after two years, is shifting the platform's focus beyond helping users build apps toward enabling them to earn money from those projects. The company reports that around 80 percent of users arrive seeking a financial incentive, such as building customer-facing platforms for online sales, yet only 35 percent currently earn revenue from their work. Osika frames this gap with the question of whether someone who likes cakes could vibe-code a living out of it—illustrating his goal of helping people run small businesses based on passions, like opening a cake shop. Cofounder and chief technology officer Fabian Hedin says Lovable is building automations to support everything from initial business strategy and website creation to long-term customer retention and marketing plans; for example, a cake shop owner would receive an AI-generated morning briefing through a chatbot-style dashboard that analyzes sales of cake boxes during holiday promotions, automatically answers customer emails, and reminds the owner to make financial deposits on time. Osika notes that vibe-coded projects have been especially valuable to social media content creators who can leverage their platforms better through sites built with Lovable, building larger businesses around their audiences—examples include a creator using it to sell their book and others selling merchandise. The startup faces an uphill battle earning the trust of these entrepreneurs because vibe-coded projects were notorious for security flaws that exposed user data on the open web; earlier this month Lovable revamped its security approach as part of making sites generated through its platform more secure by default. Igor Andriushchenko, Lovable's head of security, told WIRED: "The moment real people use what you build, security is the product." Osika will consider next year a success if he can help a new wave of entrepreneurs start sustainable businesses—"Why just vibe code an app when you can vibe code a living?"
items.title: Lovable Pivots to Help Users Vibe-Code Sustainable Businesses Amid Security Overhaul

items.summary:
Energy bills for the typical Great Britain household are projected to reach £2,166 a year from January, according to Cornwall Insight. The leading forecaster attributes this rise partly to pressure on gas and electricity prices stemming from the Middle East conflict. Its forecast indicates that the government's cap on gas and electricity prices is likely to increase by 26%, equivalent to adding £443 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, representing one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record. This prediction arrives as Ofgem prepares next Wednesday to set new energy rates for January through March via a fresh energy price cap.

The forecast stands well above Cornwall's late September projection that the cap would rise by 16% to £1,999 a year following an October increase in gas market prices. That earlier estimate had been driven by escalating violence in the Middle East and deepening fears over Europe's gas storage levels. Craig Lowrey, retail markets principal at Cornwall Insight, noted that energy bills were already climbing in October before rising again into the new year, with colder January weather pushing up consumption while households grapple with the cost of living crisis.

The price rise comes as a setback for the government after chancellor John Healey pledged to set 'a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe' in his maiden budget last month. To cushion struggling households this winter, Healey promised a one-off £100 payment in January reaching 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.

The household energy payment totals about £2.6bn and will be delivered directly into bank accounts alongside the warm home discount, which offers roughly six million means-tested households across England, Wales and Scotland a £150 reduction on winter fuel bills. The measures follow electricity levy cuts over the past year that reduced costs by around £150 annually, plus a Treasury commitment to keep the 5% VAT levy off electricity for 29 million households until July, extending annual savings of about £50.

The forecast coincides with Office for National Statistics figures showing headline inflation rose to 3.6% in October from 3.5% in September, driven by higher petrol prices and a record-high diesel price.
items.title: GB energy price cap forecast to jump 26% as Middle East conflict drives up bills

items.summary: In a housing society in West Goregaon, Mr. Jayaswal owns flat D-101 and Mrs. Nalawade owns flat D-201 within the four-wing (A, B, C, D) complex. The society originally had 40 members before an approved redevelopment plan raised membership to 215; under that plan only two flats of 1300 sq.ft each were built in the D wing, both owned by Jayaswal and Nalawade. Redevelopment was completed in 2016, and on May 20, 2018 the society asked flat owners to begin paying maintenance charges. From 2018 through 2022 each owner paid Rs 7,867 monthly; from 2022 onward the society raised Jayaswal's charge to Rs 27,166 and Nalawade's to Rs 29,266, arguing that maintaining the D wing cost more. The owners refused, contending maintenance should be calculated per flat rather than per wing, and also claimed that since July 2022 the society had withdrawn security and housekeeping services for their flats. On November 3, 2026 they won an interim case at the Maharashtra State Co-Operative Appellate Court, which ordered the society to stop collecting the enhanced amount until the dispute is resolved. Advocate Vishal Gehrana of Karanjawala & Company told ET Wealth Online that a nearly fourfold increase naturally raises questions about how the new figure was calculated and that these two members' challenge had merit at the interim stage. He said the society decided to recalculate maintenance on a wing-wise basis but failed to follow through with safeguards it had promised residents, including verification of calculations, consideration of objections before implementation, appointment of an independent Chartered Accountant, display of figures on the notice board, and hearing member concerns before finalizing revised billing. Gehrana noted that although a general body has broad authority over day-to-day affairs, this power is not unlimited; he cited the Bombay High Court's Venus Co-operative housing society ruling holding that a majority cannot use its voting power to justify an arbitrary or unreasonable demand on others. The order remains interim: the court did not declare wing-wise maintenance unlawful nor finally hold the revised charges illegal. On the record, A wing has 82 flats, B wing has 55 flats, C wing has 76 flats, and D wing has only 2 flats; it is admitted that after redevelopment these four wings were constructed by the builder. The society claimed a majority vote at an AGM dated September 30, 2018 led to a resolution passed under agenda No.4 in the AGM dated March 27, 2022, and argued this majority cannot be challenged by two members. However, the court found no copy of minutes showing that AGM approved revising maintenance; instead those minutes show the secretary proposed recalculating charges after considering actual expenses per unit, appointing a Chartered Accountant to confirm calculations, displaying them on the notice board, and finalizing revised billing only after hearing member objections. The society never held an AGM or SGM to discuss the CA-confirmed figures nor considered member objections before finalizing rates. Although the society alleged that its managing committee unanimously approved the revised calculations at a meeting on May 20, 2022, it produced no such resolution; in a co-operative society any maintenance increase must be approved by the general body, and the managing committee cannot take policy decisions without that approval. The court observed that imposing revised charges directly from July 1, 2022 was against the object of the Co-operative Act, and under Model Byelaws 2014 maintenance should be charged per flat or unit rather than wing-wise. When asked how D wing incurred higher costs, the society cited a separate water connection, electricity connection, a lift for only two flats, and use of the common compound as personal space; the court rejected these reasons as consistent with the redevelopment plan and not extraordinary facilities enjoyed by the two owners. The court held that since constructing four wings with different flat counts was the society's own decision, it could not blame the disputants for using lift, water, and electricity services sized to only two flats, nor be allowed to charge exorbitant maintenance on D wing flats.
items.title: Maharashtra Co-Operative Appellate Court halts wing-wise maintenance hike for two Goregaon flat owners

items.summary: Lucio Usobiaga of Mexico won the 2026 Basque Culinary World Prize, also called the 'Nobel Prize of Gastronomy,' for his project Arca Tierra. The prize was created in 2016 by the government of Spain's Basque autonomous region and the Basque Culinary Center, and awards 100,000 euros (about $110,000) to a winner-chosen project. Usobiaga said he wants people to know that chinampero farmers have lived in the chinampas for millennia and that their work has mostly gone unseen. Arca Tierra is described as a network of farmers and Mexico's culinary community helping preserve Xochimilco, an ancient pre-Aztec system of agricultural canal islands built into wetlands in the southern valley of Mexico City. The project cultivates 6 hectares (about 15 acres) within the chinampas and works with 50 farming families across Xochimilco, Puebla, Hidalgo, and the state of Mexico; these farms supply around 60 restaurants in Mexico City with fresh produce. Usobiaga told Food & Wine that the chinampa soil's high organic matter from lake sediments gives food grown there a special flavor, adding: 'I can tell, like from the first bite, when I'm eating a beet from the chinampas.' He cited buying products grown by chinamperos, visiting the chinampas, and paying farmers for ecosystem services as ways to support the system. Usobiaga said he also wants to attract more young people to continue farming there, noting that international recognition is helping encourage interest. The chinampas are described as the last remaining habitat for wild axolotls (Ambystoma mexicanum). Usobiaga explained their premise that 'the chinampero farmer is the guardian and custodian of the chinampas,' including its canals and animals, pointing to biofilters developed to exclude predators and clean water so axolotls can live there. He added that traditional farming and agroecology avoid toxic chemicals and help restore ecosystemic services. The article notes the chinampas filter water back to the aquifer, sequester carbon, hold biodiversity, and sustain culture; Usobiaga warned they are being lost to urbanization and abandonment while chinampero resistance remains strong but needs support in many ways. Mongabay's Aimee Gabay reported on these farmers in 2024. The banner image of Lucio Usobiaga is courtesy of Pablo Antoli.
items.title: Lucio Usobiaga Wins 2026 Basque Culinary World Prize for Protecting Mexico's Chinampas

items.summary: Andy Burnham said he would consider cutting national insurance for young people 'very carefully', but declined a firm commitment, noting that any change is a matter for the budget and must be weighed against affordability. He described reviewing all available evidence rather than ruling on policy outright. A Tuesday report by former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn proposed gradually lowering NICs paid by firms for under-25s, starting with retail and hospitality companies, and doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NICs for 21- to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. Burnham defended his predecessor Keir Starmer and former chancellor Rachel Reeves against claims that their welfare reforms were wrong, arguing his approach is 'a very different proposition' focused on supporting young people rather than the crude cuts pursued by Conservatives and Reform. He cited the Youth Guarantee as an example of employer support for taking on young people, while also acknowledging existing exemptions: no employer NICs are paid for workers younger than 21 or apprentices under 25 unless they earn above £50,270, and employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000 for non-apprentices aged 21-24. Official figures show nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, which Burnham framed as evidence that a fundamentally different, more localised approach is needed rather than a top-down tick-box system.
items.title: Burnham weighing NIC cuts to boost youth employment amid welfare reform debate

items.summary:
A new report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) finds that wildlife trafficking persists in West and Central Africa despite increased enforcement, with Nigeria remaining a central export hub for elephant ivory and pangolin scales shipped to Asia. Although enforcement operations have grown since 2020—resulting in more incidents detected, arrests, and prosecutions—the illegal trade has barely been disrupted. Traffickers relocated their operations from Lagos's Lekki Craft Market, where law enforcement presence increased, to smaller port cities with weaker oversight such as Enungu (about 230 kilometers/140 miles inland) and Port Harcourt. Criminal networks have also adapted by concealing contraband in legitimate products like edible moringa seeds and channeling illicit funds through bank transfers and underground banking systems.

The report's findings underscore the gap between enforcement activity and actual disruption: of 58 documented wildlife crime incidents in Nigeria since January 2021, only six resulted in prosecutions. Across West and Central Africa, the arrest-to-conviction rate stands at just 16%, with low-level actors such as poachers and middlemen typically taking the fall while powerful kingpins and corrupt officials avoid justice. EIA's Justin Gosling noted that Nigeria had achieved its first high-level wildlife trafficking prosecutions in years but cautioned that competing crime interests and broader economic issues limit progress.

The trade centers on pangolin scales, used in traditional Chinese medicine despite having no proven medicinal value, and elephant ivory—both highly coveted by Asian buyers. Pangolins are the world's most trafficked mammal; with Southeast Asian supplies depleted, poachers have increasingly targeted Africa, where two of four species are now endangered and two vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. All eight pangolin species received CITES protection in 2017 banning cross-border commercial sale.

By volume, Nigeria remained the region's primary exit point for illegal wildlife from 2021 to 2026, with more than 50,000 kg (more than 110,000 lb) of elephant ivory and pangolin scales seized. Gabon recorded the most wildlife crime incidents in that period, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo followed with more than 16,000 kg (about 35,000 lb) seized.

Experts warn against a 'leaking bucket' dynamic, where crackdowns simply displace trafficking to other regions. Ruth Musgrave of the Elephant Protection Initiative Foundation emphasized that enforcement agencies must prosecute the right people and disrupt networks rather than only targeting peripheral actors. Gosling stressed that preventing wildlife crime is especially critical because harm occurs at the outset—killing an animal or felling a tree—even if traffickers are later caught, leaving authorities with 'just stockrooms full of dead animals.' A glimmer of hope lies in Nigeria's forthcoming Endangered Species Conservation and Protection Bill 2024, though experts caution that such measures must be adopted and enforced across the entire region.
items.title: West and Central Africa Remain Hubs of Illegal Wildlife Trade Despite Enforcement Efforts

items.summary: Education First (EF) released its largest global ranking of adult English proficiency on Wednesday, with Japan placing 86th out of 123 countries. This represented an improvement of 10 places over the previous year, when Japan ranked 96th; that prior edition marked an all-time low and extended a downward trend in Japanese English proficiency across recent years. The 2026 index drew on test results from 2.3 million participants across 117 countries and regions. Alongside its rank improvement, Japan moved up one proficiency band this year, shifting from the lowest category, "very low," to the "low" band. Despite these gains, EF noted that Japan still trailed peers in Asia and elsewhere: it ranked 36 places below South Korea's 50th-place finish, scored 450 points versus a global average of 485 (35 points below), performed worse than European countries such as Sweden, Austria, and Denmark at the top of the rankings, and showed weaker results in speaking and writing relative to reading. EF also found regional variation within Japan, with learners in urban hubs like Yokohama, Tokyo, and Kyoto outperforming those in Hiroshima, Shizuoka, and Kochi. As across many countries covered by the index, younger Japanese adults lagged most sharply: 18- to 20-year-olds recorded the lowest scores of all age groups. EF attributed this decline partly to the COVID-19 pandemic's knock-on effects on a cohort that took online rather than in-person English classes between 2019 and 2022, an effect observed both in Japan and worldwide. In response, Masato Suzuki, business development manager for EF Japan, said raising proficiency among this generation would create a bottom-up effect as they enter the workforce; Nana Gronning Ito, EF country manager, advised against relying solely on digital learning and instead emphasized real-life communication and experiencing the joy of expression even when making mistakes. The summary reflects only what is reported in the article, including its framing that Japan's improvement does not erase continued lags behind peers.
items.title: Japan Ranks 86th in EF's 2026 Adult English Proficiency Index After Rising from a Record Low

items.summary: This document is a collection of reader letters responding to articles published in Scroll's EcoIndia section and elsewhere. One letter questions the decision to include an article about the emerging Jewish community in Andhra Pradesh, describing it as lacking literary or culinary value and suggesting it was a thinly veiled attempt at seeding Jewish ancestry; the writer also expresses doubt that the publication edited the piece and raises concerns about Israel's treatment of Palestinians before stating their ability to read Scroll with trust is broken. Another letter addresses how Rabindranath Tagore should be judged by Bangladeshis, arguing that his appeal lies in the universality of his art rather than modernity or communal identity, noting he never considered himself Hindu or Muslim but a human being who found unity amid diversity; this writer observes that whether Muslim-majority Bangladesh tolerates the cultural and spiritual dominance of a Hindu Tagore will determine his fate there. A third letter contends that Tagore has received more privilege than other Bengali poets and notes he opposed the establishment of Dhaka University following the Partition of Bengal, arguing against blind worship of him. A fourth letter discusses votebank politics in India, comparing how secular and Left parties relied on upper-caste and lower-caste Muslim support to how middle-class Hindus are treated by the Bharatiya Janata Party; the writer argues these groups remain trapped with identity and ideology and that both Hindus and Muslims will not prosper unless they confront this dynamic. A fifth letter from a 78-year-old praises election conduct, honoring Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha for setting aside Indira Gandhi's election and TN Seshan as outstanding stalwarts of independent India. Another comment references the SIR exercise in Karnataka, suggesting banks should adopt similar practices while noting many people hold multiple bank accounts; this is followed by a separate remark calling for the Supreme Court to stop centralized election software. A further letter criticizes the conduct of the Supreme Court and Chief Election Commissioner over millions of eligible voters being deprived of their rights during an election where judges reportedly only said vote next time, urging a mass movement against errant judges. The final letter responds positively to an EcoIndia episode on reviving India's repair culture to curb e-waste; it argues that forcing companies to make phones in particular ways might kill innovation or be difficult to enforce technically, and instead suggests requiring original spare parts sold openly like car service parts, starting with a battery buyback mandate for smartphones and incentives such as tax cuts for modular designs like Fairphones. The document contains no figures beyond the age of one letter's writer (78) and references to millions of eligible voters being deprived of their rights.
items.title: Readers' comments on Tagore, Jewish community cuisine, votebank politics and election conduct

items.summary: South Africa is preparing for a potentially difficult summer as the established El Niño phenomenon—defined in the article as the warming of Pacific Ocean surface temperatures that influences global weather and drives extreme events like floods, droughts, and heat waves—is expected to intensify into a very intense 'super El Niño' by late 2026, with effects continuing until early 2027. The World Meteorological Organization is cited as the source of this expectation. This super El Niño raises risks of increased drought, heat waves, water stress, pasture loss for livestock, reduced cereal yields, and forest fires in southern Africa. Researchers specializing in pastoral and crop production argue that planting dates matter significantly: their study conducted at Cedara in KwaZulu-Natal's Midlands region—characterized by deep red clay soil with hot, humid summers—showed that earlier planting (December and January) generally produced better results when forage radish was sown over a four-month period relying solely on rainfall without fertilizer. This approach reflected conditions of smallholder farmers with limited access to irrigation and fertilizers. The study found that radish planted in December produces substantially more tubers, while radish planted in January yields more leafy, higher-protein forage; mineral concentrations such as phosphorus, potassium, and zinc are also higher in leaves when planting is earlier. Higher forage nutritional value supports faster livestock growth and health, whereas farmers who cannot grow sufficient quality forage risk income losses when animals lack food. The article notes that the study was conducted over a limited period of two planting seasons within a small area of KwaZulu-Natal's Midlands, meaning results may not apply to other South African regions with different soil types, climates, and rainfall patterns, and additional trials are needed using different crops, sowing periods, and rainfall conditions. The researchers recommend that farmers plan for a range of dates rather than fixed ones, adjusting planting within a season to accommodate early or late rains, since planting too early or too late can expose young plants to drought or flooding; they also emphasize the need for agricultural advisors, weather services, and researchers to translate seasonal forecasts into practical sowing recommendations before decisions are made. The article states that even simple management decisions like timely planting help farmers use available rainfall more efficiently without purchasing expensive new equipment.
items.title: Planting Date Strategy for Forage Radish Under South African El Niño Conditions

items.summary: On November 6, 2024, Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) introduced a regulatory framework to promote the integration of battery energy storage systems (BESS) with existing solar photovoltaic installations. The guidelines establish a competitive bidding and capacity allocation mechanism for eligible grid-connected PV plants exceeding 1 MW in size. Successful applicants must install battery storage with a minimum energy capacity equivalent to 2.61 MWh per MW of rated storage power, complete installation and grid connection within 15 months, and release grid connection capacity equal to 1.5 times the rated storage power. The framework also includes provisions for a daily guaranteed billing quantity linked to 2.61 times the rated storage power capacity, subject to operational requirements. Electricity discharge will be coordinated according to national utility Taipower's scheduling and dispatch needs, shifting part of Taiwan's solar output from midday periods toward times when stored energy provides greater value. The competitive bidding mechanism determines battery capacity tariffs offered to successful applicants, introducing market-based price competition intended to improve grid infrastructure utilization and enable additional renewable integration. In January 2025, MOEA announced plans to accelerate solar and offshore wind deployment targeting an additional 8.2 GW of combined capacity by end of 2026, though deployment has progressed more slowly than anticipated. A December 2025 GlobalData forecast projected Taiwan's cumulative solar capacity would reach 31.2 GW by 2035, with the 20 GW milestone now expected in 2029; the government maintained solar feed-in tariffs for 2026 at levels set in the second half of 2025 to sustain investment and deployment. Energy storage is gaining prominence: French manufacturer Saft announced plans in October 2025 to supply 356 MWh for a Taichung project, bringing its planned installed capacity on the island to 630 MWh by 2026. Earlier examples of storage integration include a 15 MW/15 MWh battery system connected to a 150 MW solar park in southern Taiwan.
items.title: Taiwan introduces bidding framework for storage deployment at existing PV plants

items.summary: Mitch Hall and his wife Lori live in one of a few dozen town houses built so far at Veridian at County Farm, a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes there produce roughly as much solar energy as they consume, storing surplus power in batteries for evening use. In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in what will become Michigan's first residential virtual power plant (VPP) pilot; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy would then remotely control residents' home batteries to inject stored solar onto the grid when operators need it most. Joi Harris, president and CEO of DTE Energy, said in a statement that 'this pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,' noting VPPs can smooth demand peaks and reduce reliance on expensive fossil-fuel peaker plants and grid-infrastructure upgrades. Residents would also be compensated: Matt Hall said DTE 'will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.' The utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and prices are likely highest, so residents need not optimize usage themselves; however, exact compensation figures were unavailable because DTE did not respond to Canary Media's request in time for publication. VPPs have existed for years but gained traction slowly due to lack of utility incentives and high costs of home solar and batteries, though electrification and a data center rush are now driving demand growth. Earlier this month the Brattle Group estimated that 524 gigawatts of distributed energy resources in VPPs could save households an average of $122 per year by 2050. Kevin Brehm, manager in the carbon-free electricity practice at clean energy think tank RMI, said 'there's immense untapped capacity.' Matt Grocoff, founder of Thrive Collaborative, began considering a VPP pilot at Veridian in 2019 to mimic an ecosystem where homes produce their own energy and share it mutually across a network rather than through a one-directional grid; he described how each home 'can be producing energy that it needs and mutually beneficially sharing it across a network of energy.' DTE expects nearly 100 battery-equipped Veridian homes to participate, with the pilot expected to deliver up to about 300 kilowatts for three hours. So far, 44 market-rate homes with solar and batteries have been built out of 120 planned, as have 50 affordable housing units without batteries yet, according to Thrive Collaborative. Battery manufacturer Sonnen USA supplies the home storage systems and is helping DTE operate the pilot using its proprietary software; Geoff Ferrell, executive vice president of Sonnen USA's VPP business unit, called Veridian 'a test bed.' He pointed to a similar Sonnen-facilitated program that began in 2017 at Soleil Lofts outside Salt Lake City with solar on a new apartment building. Rocky Mountain Power and the state utility commission extended the initial program to every residential customer after promising early data; today about 7,900 homes and businesses participate under the name Wattsmart Battery across Utah, Wyoming, and Idaho. Brehm would like more utilities to launch at full scale given numerous existing programs to model on, but noted Rocky Mountain Power's pilot is a good example for cautious utilities because its employees quickly understood how the residential battery fleet works and could integrate it into operations and resource-capacity planning; he'd like DTE to do likewise. The Veridian VPP pilot has already inspired developers and utilities outside Michigan, including Peace Hill in Townsend, Washington, according to Grocoff, who said 'we're getting calls from all over the country.'
items.title: Veridian at County Farm to become Michigan's first virtual power plant pilot

items.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola has won the closely contested Alaska Senate race, marking a decisive victory for Democrats in the US upper house. The win delivered the party's 56th Senate seat and became its ninth pickup from Republicans this cycle, giving them control of Congress for the remainder of Donald Trump's presidency alongside their regained House majority. Calling Peltola two weeks after counting began reflected Alaska's logistical difficulty collecting ballots across its remote territory; with 99% counted she held slightly more than 50%, while incumbent Dan S Sullivan trailed on under 46%. In her victory statement, Peltola said the 'status quo in DC is not working for Alaska,' recalling rural Alaskans facing hardship and pledging to fight corporate greed and put Alaska first. The race was complicated by an alleged effort reported by the New York Times to recruit a political unknown named Daniel J Sullivan—sharing a name with incumbent Dan S Sullivan—to confuse voters; after legal challenges, state courts allowed him on the ballot while election officials distinguished them in materials. Peltola denied knowledge of any plot, and both the justice department and Alaska's Republican governor announced investigations into her campaign. The Trump administration filed suit to block certification if incumbent Sullivan lost, but a federal judge dismissed it following challenges from Alaska election officials, the Peltola campaign, and voting groups. Because Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, confused voters could rank each Dan Sullivan first and second; after the non-incumbent candidate was eliminated, his votes would reallocate to the incumbent, limiting any spoiler's impact—analysis by BBC Verify found Peltola would still have won even if every vote for the other Daniel J Sullivan had gone to him. The seat began as a must-win toss-up but became surplus once Democrats secured enough seats nationally.
items.title: Mary Peltola Wins Alaska Senate Seat in Contested Midterm Race

items.summary: The article centers on how climate change is making app-based delivery work in New York City increasingly dangerous, while documenting the workers' own organizing to improve their conditions. José Yos, a 40-year-old Guatemalan food-and-grocery deliverista who rides e-bikes for apps like DoorDash (element_id: entity-502-510), describes riding through wildfire smoke from Quebec wildfires in Canada on sweltering days during the city's second heat emergency of two weeks, when temperatures were projected to reach close to 100 degrees Fahrenheit with an even higher heat index. He wore a balaclava and kept working because he had reserved his Uber Eats hours ahead and feared losing his rating or being deactivated if deliveries slowed (element_id: entity-1364-1373). Before the city's deactivation protection bill enacted in January 2026, workers could be removed from apps without cause; now apps must give 72 hours' notice before deactivating a worker and have the action investigated. Yos nonetheless avoided triggering that process (element_id: date-1611-1615). He said weather affects him in two ways — risking health and safety while putting his livelihood on the line, since apps do not grant extra time to pick up or drop off orders when conditions are bad, which lowers ratings. Of roughly 70,000 delivery workers across the five boroughs (element_id: quantity-3412-3427), many hail from Latin America, with a growing number being migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — regions facing climate change's brunt; Guatemala has suffered droughts and flooding that suppressed crop yields, linked to both climate change and El Niño patterns. As gig-economy freelancers, these workers lack adequate health and safety protections.
items.title: Climate change intensifies dangers for New York's migrant delivery workers amid labor organizing and adaptation efforts

items.summary:
The article opens by noting that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid reports of two extramarital relationships, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, and his public admission of being unfaithful to wife Lori Mills. While this drew attention to the personal life of a billionaire ranking 16th on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index with an estimated net worth of $130 billion, it also spotlighted the financial scale of high-profile divorces. The piece then surveys five such settlements.

Bill Gates and Melinda French Gates separated in May 2021 after nearly 27 years of marriage. NDTV Profit reported that Melinda received more than $2 billion in shares, though exact terms remain undisclosed. In 2024 she announced leaving the Gates Foundation under an agreement worth $12.5 billion for her philanthropic work; although this was not part of a publicly confirmed divorce settlement, reports put the combined value of their financial arrangements at more than $14.5 billion. The couple agreed to divide marital assets, and Melinda did not seek spousal support.

Jeff Bezos divorced MacKenzie Scott in July 2019 after 25 years of marriage. As part of the settlement, Scott received about 4% of Amazon's total outstanding shares — 19.7 million shares valued at approximately $38.3 billion at the time. Bezos retained a 12% stake and control over the voting rights attached to the transferred shares. Scott later committed through the Giving Pledge to donate at least half of her wealth to charity; the settlement was notable for transferring a substantial company stake rather than being limited to cash.

French-American art dealer Alec Wildenstein married Jocelyn in 1978 and divorced in 1999 after 21 years. Jocelyn reportedly received an initial $2.5 billion, followed by annual payments of $100 million for 13 years, bringing the combined reported settlement to approximately $3.8 billion. Wildenstein died in 2008.

Rupert Murdoch divorced journalist Anna Murdoch in 1999 after nearly three decades of marriage and had three children together. Their settlement was widely reported at $1.7 billion, much associated with News Corporation shares, though exact terms were never disclosed and the figure has been questioned; it was structured to protect his control over his business empire.

Bill Gross, co-founder of Pacific Investment Management Company (PIMCO), married Sue Gross in 1985. They separated in 2016 after more than three decades when Sue filed for divorce in November that year. She reportedly received assets worth $1.3 billion, including a $36 million property in Laguna Beach and half of the couple's art collection.

The article concludes that these divorces — spanning company shares, investment assets, and court awards — demonstrate how high-profile separations carry significant financial consequences, even as several exact terms remain private. The piece is written by Swati Gandhi, a digital journalist with over four years' experience covering international and geopolitical issues for Business Standard and Live Mint.
items.title: Five of the world's most expensive billionaire divorce settlements

items.summary: The Karnataka High Court on Tuesday stayed investigations into three cases against 10 persons accused of fraudulently using Form 7s of the Election Commission to delete Muslim voters during a special intensive revision of electoral rolls, per Bar and Bench. Form 7 is used to object to inclusion or seek deletion of names from an electoral roll. The FIRs were filed after complainants alleged that Form 7s had been submitted in bulk based on false information, forged signatures, and impersonation to remove eligible electors, mainly Muslims, from voter lists. In October, the court had stayed probes in two other similar cases; Tuesday's order extended the stay to three more cases involving 10 accused persons. The Congress-led state government opposed the petitions seeking a stay, contending that the right to vote is extremely valuable and that fake or forged forms cannot be allowed. Petitioners argued instead that booth-level agents are entitled to file Form 7s on behalf of political parties during electoral roll preparation and revision, complementing the Election Commission's booth level officers, and that correctness should be examined by the electoral registration officer. The court directed the poll panel to place materials relating to decisions taken on Form 7 use on record, observing that the statutory inquiry into their correctness under the 1960 Registration of Electors Rules must first be completed before any police investigation is warranted. That same rules framework provides for imprisonment of up to one year, a fine, or both, for knowingly making a false written declaration; the bench noted these provisions while examining scrutiny and hearing procedures. The stay thus defers criminal action pending completion of that inquiry. This case sits within a broader national revision exercise: its first phase ran in Bihar in 2025, was extended to 12 states and Union Territories in late 2025 and the first half of 2026 as a second phase, and a third phase is underway across 19 states and Union Territories. Since it began, concerns have been raised that revision could eliminate genuine voters or shape electoral outcomes; Scroll reported on these worries. In May, the Supreme Court upheld the legality of the revision but said it does not permit the Election Commission to decide whether a person is an Indian citizen. Despite this, Bharatiya Janata Party-ruled states have cited the SIR to deny ration cards to those eliminated from rolls, and in some cases police denied passport renewal permission. Since October 2, nationwide protests calling for resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar have been held over concerns about the Commission's functioning and alleged irregularities in roll revision.
items.title: Karnataka HC stays police probe in three Form 7 fraud cases over Muslim voter deletions

items.summary:
The Senate is poised to pass a "permitting reform" bill called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which would streamline federal permit processes for large infrastructure projects. The motivation stems from delays that have slowed renewable energy development: the SunZia wind farm transmission line in New Mexico, described as the largest renewable project ever built in the United States, took two decades to construct and remains entangled in unresolved court battles over impacts on historic sites even after completion in June. Such legal challenges are said to threaten long-distance power line construction nationwide.

At its core, BAAJA would speed up environmental and historic preservation reviews under laws including the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) and the National Historic Preservation Act by narrowing what agencies must consider, restricting who can sue over those reviews, and shortening deadlines. Companies argue permits are time-consuming, unpredictable, and costly; opponents say this reduces public scrutiny and makes it harder for communities and tribes to identify harms or protect sacred sites.

The bill also targets the power grid specifically: giving federal authorities greater ability to override states that block interstate lines, requiring regional operators to approve reliability-improving lines, and preventing states from using the Clean Water Act to block crossings unless they directly discharge into water. It would not affect most projects on private land within one state.

On communities, experts expect reduced power for tribes, states, and local groups to delay or scrutinize projects, alongside slightly lower electricity costs over 15 years as cheap regional power moves more easily and rooftop solar sales improve. Most data centers are expected to see little change because they sit on private land under state oversight; the bill could still accelerate their supporting infrastructure while requiring them to pay for grid upgrades and increasing transparency around electricity use.

On climate, BAAJA would enable both fossil fuel and renewable projects, with some projections favoring renewables due to faster permitting and expanded transmission. Rhodium Group models modest emissions reductions even if natural gas prices fall more than renewables, with larger cuts if renewables become much cheaper; the firm also expects natural gas pipelines to continue at roughly their current pace while renewable deployment accelerates. A key concern is that Republicans could exploit faster permitting for fossil fuels, though amendments attempt to limit presidential discrimination among energy sources—provisions some opponents say are too weak and others worry may be too strong.

Supporters include labor unions, clean and fossil energy companies, a few tribes, centrist policy organizations, and climate groups. Notably, Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich co-wrote the bill while opposing it did Green New Deal sponsors Ed Markey and Mazie Hirono; Al Gore and Genevieve Guenther oppose it, while Zeke Hausfather and David Pomerantz support it. The split has divided Democrats and the climate movement: some opponents favor permitting reform but want to wait until January for majorities in both houses to add stronger protections.

Legislatively, BAAJA is likely to pass the Republican-controlled Senate—where nearly every Republican and half of Democrats have advanced it—and could leave that chamber before Thanksgiving if amendments don't derail it. Its future in the House is more uncertain: crafted with limited input from members there, some Republicans including Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie express concern over transmission provisions, rural lawmakers may resist ceding local influence, and House Democrats such as Hakeem Jeffries have voiced concerns that could allow a coalition to defeat it. Trump supports permitting reform; if the bill isn't signed before year's end, it dies and would require starting over next session.
items.title: Congress’ energy permitting bill and what it means for communities, costs, and climate

items.summary: The States of Deliberation is set to decide next week whether to temporarily reduce 2027 social insurance contributions by 0.5%, lowering employee (primary Class 1) rates to 7.1% and self-employed (Class 2) rates to 12.1%. The proposal would apply to both employees and the self-employed, according to Forward Guernsey deputies Gavin St Pier and Tom Rylatt, who intend to bring an amendment to the Social Insurance (Rates of Contributions and Benefits etc.) Ordinance, 2026. St Pier cited global events, including the Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran wars, as having created significant economic pressures across the community on Guernsey. He noted that contributions have risen each year under a 10-year programme of increases; without this amendment, employee contributions would have increased by 1% since 2021 and self-employed contributions by 1.6%. Rylatt said the cut would give working islanders "breathing room," arguing that with little sign of cost-of-living pressures easing in 2027 and tax reform now decided, this year is a suitable time to use the flexibility built into the Employment and Social Security (ESS) 10-year plan. He estimated the amendment for 2027 would amount to a loss of between £8m and £9m for the Guernsey Insurance Fund, but described it as "a one-off departure from the existing trajectory." The article reports no vote outcome or further detail beyond this proposal.
items.title: Guernsey States to debate a cut in 2027 social security contributions
